In the Greek New Testament, it occurs ten times, appearing in passages that warn against sinful living and describe behavior associated with life apart from God. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is unrestrained moral excess rather than an ordinary weakness or isolated mistake.

The surrounding verse determines how that condition functions in the passage, but the word itself expresses being exposed or dressed in rags.

The precise force in any sentence depends on what the word describes, but its central idea is unending duration and lasting permanence.

Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the same: openly mocking or deriding someone. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew and Luke, and is rendered “when” in each recorded occurrence. Its exact force in a sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central function is to identify timing or sequence.
